title: Literature in the Language Classroom

points.h: Why Use Literature at This Level
pts: Literary texts offer linguistic richness, cultural insight, and genuine emotional engagement in combination few other authentic texts match.
This extends Unit 41's authentic-materials principle into one of its most demanding and rewarding text types.
C1 learners typically have the linguistic base to engage with literature meaningfully, without needing heavy simplification.
points.who: Ronald Carter & Michael Long's work on literature in language teaching

v: One short literary text and one authentic factual text on the same theme

items: Choose a short literary text (a poem or a one-page story) and a factual text on the same theme, such as migration to the city.
Read both and list what each offers: vocabulary, grammar, cultural insight, emotional engagement, discussion potential.
Match your list to Carter and Long’s (1991) three models: cultural, language and personal growth.
Decide which model you mainly use at present, and which you neglect.
Plan one lesson in which the literary text is used for all three purposes.
In a DIET or cluster meeting, colleagues each bring one text and present its case in two minutes.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A teacher’s notes on two texts about leaving a village (fictional notes):

lines: Factual text: clear facts on urban migration; useful statistics vocabulary; little emotional pull.
Poem: metaphor of roots; tense shifts between past village and present city; strong feeling; many possible readings.
Model I neglect: personal growth. I usually ask only comprehension questions.

blocks.x: Advanced learners usually have the linguistic base to engage with such texts without heavy simplification. This extends the authentic-materials principle of Unit 41 to one of its richest text types.

body: Purpose: to show Carter and Long’s three models. Content: a book at the centre with three paths leading from it to a globe (culture), a magnifying glass over words (language) and a growing plant (personal growth). Style: clean, warm. Board version: a rectangle with three labelled arrows.

items: Project Gutenberg (free) for public-domain literary texts in English.

blocks.x: The school library and state textbooks’ literary sections.

pts: Select texts based on linguistic accessibility, thematic relevance, and length appropriate to available class time — not literary canon status alone.
Short stories and poetry often suit classroom time constraints better than novel-length texts, without sacrificing genuine literary value.
This connects to Unit 41's task-grading principle — grade the task around a genuinely rich text rather than simplifying the text itself.

v: Three or four candidate texts; a selection checklist

items: List candidate texts, including at least one short story, one poem and one extract from Indian writing in English or in translation.
Rate each on four criteria: linguistic accessibility, thematic relevance to your learners, length relative to class time, and copyright status.
Discard any text that scores low on accessibility and relevance together.
For the remaining texts, design tasks at two levels of demand rather than simplifying the text.
Choose one text to trial and note learners’ reactions.
Invite learners to nominate texts from their own reading, in English or other languages, and apply the same checklist together.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Grading the task, not the text, for one poem:

lines: Easier task: Find three words connected with water. How does the poem make you feel?
Harder task: How does the poet’s use of the present tense in the last stanza change the meaning of the first?

Sarojini Naidu, ‘In the Bazaars of Hyderabad’ (1912): accessible vocabulary with a glossary of ten items; strong local relevance; fits one 40-minute lesson; public domain [VERIFY public-domain status in the reader’s jurisdiction].

blocks.x: Short stories and poems usually suit timetable constraints better than novels, without losing literary value.

points.sub: Language as the object of study
pts: Stylistics examines how a literary text's specific linguistic choices create meaning and effect.
This gives learners an analytical vocabulary for discussing language deliberately, not just consuming a text passively.
This connects directly to Unit 52's discourse and cohesion work, applied to literary, rather than purely functional, texts.
points.who: Stylistics as an approach to literary language analysis

v: A short poem or prose extract (written for this book)

items: Learners read the text once for general meaning and say in one sentence what it is about.
On a second reading, they mark anything that stands out: repetition, unusual word order, a shift in tense or pronoun, unexpected vocabulary.
In pairs, they choose two marked features and ask: what effect does this create?
The teacher introduces the term foregrounding for patterns that stand out.
Pairs rewrite one line ‘normally’ and compare the effect with the original.
Compare a feature of the English text with a similar device in a poem learners know in their home language, such as repetition in a Kannada vachana or a refrain in a Hindi film song.
Support: provide a list of features to look for.
Challenge: learners use terms such as point of view and free indirect speech in their analysis (Short 1996).

blocks.x: A short poem (written for this book):

lines: The city wakes before the sun.
The city wakes, the buses run.
My mother’s village sleeps till six;
The city wakes. The city ticks.
T: What stands out?
S1: ‘The city wakes’ three times.
S2: The village is only once. And it ‘sleeps’.
T: What effect does the repetition have?
S1: The city is always busy. It doesn’t stop, like a clock. ‘Ticks’.
T: Try it without repetition: ‘The city wakes early and is busy.’ What is lost?

blocks.x: Stylistics treats these choices as evidence for interpretation (Widdowson 1975). It builds on the cohesion work of Unit 52, applied to a literary rather than a functional text.

body: Purpose: to illustrate foregrounding. Content: the four lines of the poem with the repeated phrase highlighted, and a clock face faintly in the background; one line (the village) printed in a softer tone. Style: typographic, quiet. Board version: the poem written with the repeated phrase underlined.

items: Voyant Tools (free) to show word frequencies and repetitions in a longer text.

blocks.x: The poem written on the board with coloured chalk for patterns.

body: Deviation from ordinary language is only one way a text foregrounds meaning. Unexpected regularity, such as repeated structures or sounds, is equally important, and learners often notice it first because it is easy to see on the page.

pts: Literary texts convey cultural perspectives and values in a way factual cultural content rarely achieves as vividly.
This connects to Unit 24's intercultural competence work, adding a genuinely rich, human dimension to that earlier content.
Frame literary cultural content as one perspective, not a comprehensive or singular representation of a culture.

v: A short story or extract that shows a cultural practice

items: Learners read a story extract that depicts a family or community practice.
They note what the text shows about the characters’ values and relationships.
In groups, they discuss: is this how everyone in this culture lives? Whose perspective is shown? Whose is missing?
Learners compare with a practice from their own community, noting similarities as well as differences.
Each group writes one sentence beginning ‘This story shows one view of…’.
Pair an English-language story from another country with a story from an Indian language in translation on the same theme (a wedding, a first job, an exam result).
Support: provide guiding questions about the characters’ choices.
Challenge: learners find a second text that shows a different perspective on the same culture.

lines: S1: In this story, the grandmother decides everything. So in this culture, old people decide.
S2: But it’s one family. In my family my father decides, not my grandmother.
T: So what can we say about the story?
S1: It shows one family’s way, not the whole culture.
T: Exactly. Literature gives us a person, not a statistic.

blocks.x: Literary texts convey values more vividly than factual cultural information, but each is one perspective, not a complete picture. This extends the intercultural competence work of Unit 24.

body: Purpose: to show literature as one perspective among many. Content: a house with several windows; through each, a different family scene is visible; a reader stands at one window only. Style: gentle illustration. Board version: a rectangle with several small squares, one highlighted.

items: Internet Archive (free) for older translated Indian short stories in the public domain.

blocks.x: Photocopied extracts within fair-dealing limits, or teacher-read passages.

pts: Personal response tasks — reactions, connections, interpretations — engage learners more deeply than comprehension-check questions alone.
This connects to Unit 27's discourse competence and Unit 63's own stylistic analysis, combined with genuine affective engagement.
Structured discussion formats (Unit 39) work well for sharing and comparing personal literary interpretations.

items: Learners read the story at home or in class.
In groups of four, each learner takes a role: Connector (links to own life), Questioner (asks open questions), Word Finder (chooses memorable language), Summarizer.
Each prepares brief notes, then leads a three-minute discussion from their role.
Groups agree on one interpretation they disagree about and present both sides to the class.
Rotate roles for the next text.
Use a fishbowl format (Unit 39): one group discusses while others observe and then comment.
Support: give sentence starters for each role.
Challenge: add a Stylistician role that links one linguistic choice to an effect, using point 3 of this unit.

lines: Connector: This reminded me of… / I have felt like this when…
Questioner: Why do you think the narrator…? / What would have happened if…?
Word Finder: I chose this phrase because…
A: I think the ending is happy. She leaves the village and starts again.
B: I think it’s sad. She loses her family.
T: Both readings are supported by the text. Can you each find a line that supports yours?

blocks.x: Response-based approaches draw on Louise Rosenblatt’s (1978) view that meaning is made in the transaction between reader and text.

body: Purpose: to show structured literary discussion. Content: four learners seated around a book, each with a small role icon (a link, a question mark, a word card, a summary list) and speech bubbles meeting in the centre. Style: warm, inclusive. Board version: a circle with four labelled points.

items: Padlet (free plan, limited boards) for posting responses before discussion.

blocks.x: Role cards written on scrap paper and rotated each week.

pts: Literary texts often provide rich, memorable contextual exposure to vocabulary that extensive reading (Unit 31) reinforces at scale.
This is a natural complement to, not a replacement for, graded extensive reading's volume-based vocabulary benefits.
Literary vocabulary work benefits from Unit 5's depth-over-breadth principle — a smaller set explored richly, rather than a long glossary.

items: After reading, each learner chooses five words or phrases that seemed important or striking.
In groups, learners agree on a shared list of five.
For each item, they explore meaning in context, other meanings, collocations, connotation and a translation into a home language.
They write a new sentence using each item in a different context.
Items are added to learners’ vocabulary notebooks and recycled later in extensive reading (Unit 31).
Learners compare connotations across languages: does the Kannada or Tamil equivalent carry the same feeling?
Support: the teacher pre-selects ten items for groups to choose from.
Challenge: learners find the same items in a corpus to compare literary and everyday use.

blocks.x: One item explored in depth (from the poem at point 3):

lines: ticks: literal (a clock), figurative (a city that runs mechanically), collocations (tick away, what makes someone tick), connotation (routine, time pressure), Hindi comparison (tik-tik, a sound word).
T: Why is ‘ticks’ better than ‘works’ in the last line?
S1: It sounds like a clock. The city is like a machine.

blocks.x: A smaller set explored richly is better than a long glossary (Unit 5). Literature complements, but does not replace, the volume of extensive reading.

body: Purpose: to show depth over breadth in vocabulary. Content: on the left, a long, shallow list of twenty words; on the right, five words each with a deep root system showing meanings, collocations and connotations. Style: clear contrast. Board version: a short list with branching lines from each word.

items: Quizlet (free basic version) for learner-made cards with example sentences.

blocks.x: A vocabulary notebook page per word, with four boxes for meaning, collocation, connotation and translation.

body: Let learners choose some of the words. Items learners select for themselves are more likely to be remembered than items the teacher decides are important, and their choices tell you what they noticed.

pts: Creative response tasks (continuing a story, writing from another character's perspective) build genuine, engaged production practice.
Analytical response tasks (a literary essay) connect directly to Unit 61's academic writing and argumentation principles.
Both response types can coexist across a unit, serving different skill-development goals.

items: Offer two task types after reading: creative (write the next scene, or the story from another character’s point of view) and analytical (a short literary essay answering an interpretive question).
Model each briefly: show a short creative extension and a paragraph of literary argument.
Learners choose one task, or do the creative task first and the analytical task later in the unit.
For the analytical task, learners use the claim–evidence–response structure of Unit 61, with quotations as evidence.
Learners share their writing in small groups and discuss how each task helped them understand the text.
Learners write a letter from one character to another, or a diary entry in the voice of a minor character.
Support: provide a paragraph frame for the analytical task.
Challenge: the creative piece must imitate one stylistic feature of the original.

blocks.x: An analytical paragraph (written for this book), about the poem at point 3:

lines: The poem contrasts the city and the village through repetition. ‘The city wakes’ appears three times, while the village is mentioned only once and ‘sleeps’. This imbalance suggests that the speaker’s present life is dominated by the city’s rhythm, although the reference to the mother may hint at a continuing emotional tie.

blocks.x: A creative extension (written for this book):

lines: At six, in the village, my mother lights the stove. At six, in the city, I have already missed my bus.

body: Purpose: to show two response types. Content: an open book with two paths: one leads to a pen and a notebook labelled ‘creative’ with a small speech bubble; the other leads to a structured page with a quotation box labelled ‘analytical’. Style: balanced. Board version: a book with two arrows.

items: Google Docs (free) for drafting and peer comments.

blocks.x: Writing in notebooks with peer comments on slips of paper.

pts: Assess the quality of interpretation and language use, not a single 'correct' reading of an inherently open text.
This connects to Unit 46's rubric-design principles, calibrated for a task type where legitimate interpretive range is expected.
Clear criteria distinguishing a well-supported interpretation from an unsupported one keep assessment fair despite this openness.

v: Four learner responses to the same text (anonymized, with consent)

items: Draft criteria that do not assume one correct reading: interpretation supported by evidence, depth of engagement, use of textual detail, and language control.
Write descriptors that distinguish a well-supported interpretation from an unsupported one (Unit 46).
Score four responses independently with a colleague, including two that reach opposite interpretations.
Discuss differences and agree benchmarks.
Share the criteria with learners before their next response task.
Learners use the criteria to assess an anonymized response before writing their own.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Descriptors for ‘interpretation supported by evidence’ (written for this book):

lines: 4: A clear interpretation, consistently supported by specific textual detail; alternative readings acknowledged.
3: A clear interpretation with some textual support.
2: An interpretation stated but largely unsupported, or mostly retelling.
1: Retelling only; no interpretation.
A: This student says the ending is happy. I think it’s sad.
B: But look, she quotes two lines and explains them. That’s a 4 under our criteria.
A: You’re right. I was marking my reading, not hers.

body: Purpose: to show fair assessment of open tasks. Content: several different interpretations shown as paths leading to the same text, each path marked with footprints labelled ‘evidence’; one path without footprints is faded. Style: clean, metaphorical. Board version: a circle with several arrows, some solid, one dotted.

items: Google Sheets (free) for comparing scores across raters.

blocks.x: Photocopied responses and a paper scoring grid.

body: Choose one short poem and teach it twice: once with comprehension questions only, and once with a noticing task and response circles. Collect one written response after each lesson and compare the length, originality and use of textual evidence.

dek: Unit 63 of 100: using authentic literary texts for advanced language development — a rich, under-used resource for discourse, culture, and genuine engagement.

aims.x: Many teachers of English in India first came to the language through literature, yet in many classrooms literature has become a set of ‘lessons’ to be summarized and memorized for examinations. This unit argues for a different use: literary texts as rich, authentic language input that invites close attention to how language works, genuine personal response, and cultural reflection. It offers procedures for choosing texts, stylistic analysis, response, vocabulary, writing and fair assessment with advanced learners.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain the linguistic, cultural and personal-growth arguments for using literature with advanced learners;
select literary texts for accessibility, relevance and length, and grade the task rather than the text;
lead a simple stylistic analysis that links linguistic choices to effects;
use literature for intercultural reflection while avoiding single-story representations;
design personal-response tasks and structured literary discussions;
teach vocabulary from literary texts in depth rather than through long glossaries;
set creative and analytical writing tasks in response to literature;
assess literary response with criteria that allow for legitimate interpretive range.

why: Why this matters. Literature offers language density, cultural insight, and emotional engagement few other text types combine as richly — but it needs deliberate, informed pedagogical handling.

background.x: Literature fell out of favour in communicative language teaching during the 1970s, when it was often seen as difficult, remote and unrelated to learners’ practical needs. It returned through the 1980s and 1990s in a new form. Ronald Carter and Michael Long (1991) described three models: a cultural model, in which literature is a window on the values of a society; a language model, in which literary texts are a source of language to be studied; and a personal growth model, in which reading literature develops the learner as a reader and a person. Joanne Collie and Stephen Slater (1987) and Gillian Lazar (1993) produced widely used resource books that showed how to make literary texts active classroom material.

A key link between language and literature is stylistics: the study of how a text’s linguistic choices create meaning and effect. H. G. Widdowson (1975) argued that stylistics could bridge the gap between language teaching and literary study, and Mick Short (1996) developed practical methods for exploring poems, plays and prose. Stylistics gives learners concepts such as foregrounding (patterns that stand out, through repetition or deviation from the norm), point of view and speech presentation, which they can use to talk about language deliberately.

Research on literature in language learning is more modest than enthusiasts might hope. Amos Paran’s (2008) survey found a growing but still limited body of empirical studies, and called for more. Teachers should therefore present the benefits as well argued and promising rather than proven in every respect. What is clear is that literary texts offer dense, memorable language in context and invite the kind of personal engagement that motivates reading (Hall 2015).

India has an unusually rich resource here. Learners live among several literary traditions, including Kannada vachanas, Tamil Sangam poetry, Urdu ghazals and Hindi short stories, and there is a large body of Indian writing in English and in translation. NEP 2020 recommends the study of Indian languages and literature and supports translation (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020), and NCF 2023 sees literature as part of language education at every stage (NCERT 2023). A teacher who invites learners to compare an English poem with a poem they know in Telugu or Marathi is using the whole repertoire, not diluting the English lesson (Unit 71). A practical note: many modern texts are in copyright, so this unit uses public-domain texts or samples written for this book, and advises sharing copyrighted texts only within the limits of educational fair dealing.

items: Stylistic commentary. A short commentary linking two linguistic features of an unseen text to their effects.
Response portfolio. A collection of personal, creative and analytical responses to texts read across a term.
Discussion contribution. Observation of learners’ contributions in response circles, using role-based criteria.
Literary essay. An analytical paragraph or short essay scored with criteria for supported interpretation, not a single correct reading.
Which of Carter and Long’s three models dominates your use of literature? Why?
How much of your literature teaching asks for recall, and how much for response?
Which literary texts in your learners’ home languages could be brought into dialogue with English texts?
How do you respond when a learner’s interpretation differs from yours but is well supported?
What copyright limits apply to the texts you want to use, and how do you work within them?
When did a literary text last change how you saw something? Could it do the same for your learners?

terms.def: The associations and feelings a word carries beyond its basic meaning; for example, slim and skinny both mean thin but differ in connotation.
An approach to teaching literature that treats texts as a means of understanding the culture, history and values from which they come (Carter and Long 1991).

In stylistics, making a feature of a text stand out through repetition, parallelism or deviation from normal usage, such as unusual word order or a sudden change of tense (Short 1996). Learners discuss what effect it creates.

Adjusting the difficulty of what learners must do with a text rather than simplifying the text itself. With an authentic notice, for example, weaker learners find three facts while stronger learners interpret its tone.
The set of reasonable interpretations a literary text allows. Assessment criteria for literary response should reward well-supported readings within this range rather than one ‘correct’ answer.

In literature teaching, the model that uses literary texts to develop learners’ language knowledge and awareness (Carter and Long 1991). It is one of three models, with the cultural and personal growth models.
An approach to teaching literature that uses texts to engage learners’ emotions, experiences and personal responses, aiming at development as readers and people (Carter and Long 1991).
The perspective from which a story is told, such as first-person or third-person narration; discussing it helps learners interpret literary texts.

An approach to literature that treats meaning as made in the interaction between reader and text, so learners’ personal responses become the starting point for discussion (Rosenblatt 1978). A class might share reactions to a Kannada or English poem before analysing it.

The study of style in texts using linguistic analysis, examining how choices of words, grammar, sound and structure create meaning and effect, particularly in literature. It links language study and literary response.
